segmentos.texto: About eighty-three miles off Puerto Rico, a U.S. island, lies the deepest point in the Atlantic Ocean. It's more than five miles down. Stand Mount Everest on the bottom, and its top one thousand five hundred feet would stick out of the water. When you think "deepest ocean," you think Mariana. But that's the Pacific, about nine thousand five hundred miles away.

In nineteen sixty-four, a crew in a French deep-diving craft descended into the Puerto Rico Trench and reported a crowd of fish. In twenty nineteen, a submersible went back to the exact same spot. It saw none of those fish. The first person to reach the deepest point itself got there only in December twenty eighteen. And a twenty nineteen study found that the official list of undersea features still had the Atlantic more than one thousand feet too deep, even after sonar showed otherwise. So what is really down there, and how did anyone find out? You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of the bottom of the Atlantic begins.

On January twenty-seventh, eighteen eighty-three, a steamer called the Blake, from the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, lowered a weighted wire into the sea north of Puerto Rico. Its commander was a Navy officer named Brownson. The wire went down more than five miles before it touched bottom. That was about sixty miles east of the deepest point the sonar would later find.

The wire came back up with a sample of the seafloor and a reading of the water temperature down there. The Survey's report for that year describes the bottom as brown ooze. At the time, no one was known to have brought back a sample and a temperature from that deep.

The trench itself had been found less than a decade earlier, by the British research ship HMS Challenger, under Captain Nares, far to the east. Its sounding there, the depth it measured, came to about twenty-three thousand feet. The trench runs for hundreds of miles, almost parallel to Puerto Rico's north coast.

In nineteen thirty-nine, the cruiser USS Milwaukee bounced sound off the bottom north of Puerto Rico. It reported more than twenty-eight thousand feet, a record for the Atlantic at the time. The spot was named the Milwaukee Deep, after the ship. That summer, newspapers printed the news in a bulletin from the National Geographic Society. A sound could give a number. It couldn't show anyone what was down there.

In nineteen sixty-four, people went down into the trench themselves. They rode in a French bathyscaphe, a deep-diving craft, called Archimède. It went more than four miles down. The sources disagree on exactly how deep it got. It never reached the deepest point, though. About twenty-four thousand feet down, its crew reported a crowd of fish. They counted some two hundred of them along roughly a mile of seafloor. The report, published the next year, described them as snailfish, a family of fish. Keep those fish in mind.

NOAA, the U.S. ocean and weather agency, reports that in nineteen seventy a net brought back a small cusk-eel. A cusk-eel is a fish shaped like an eel, and this one was about eight inches long. The Australian Museum lists the same catch, from the Puerto Rico Trench. The net had gone down nearly as deep as the deepest point of the Atlantic. No one knows how deep the fish was when it swam in. A crew could see only a small patch of the trench, and a net could only bring something up. Neither could map the floor. That took a different kind of sonar.

In two thousand two and two thousand three, the U.S. Geological Survey mapped the trench with multibeam sonar, a ship's sonar that maps the seafloor in a wide strip. It took three cruises on a NOAA ship, the Ron Brown. By the end, those surveys showed the deepest part of the trench at about twenty-seven thousand three hundred feet. That was fifteen years before anyone reached the deepest point.

Why is the trench so deep? Earth's outer shell is made of giant slabs called plates. In the Pacific, deep trenches lie where one plate sinks under another. Along this trench, the North American plate and the Caribbean plate mostly slide past each other, with only a little of one sinking under the other. The Caribbean plate moves east about three-quarters of an inch a year. According to the USGS, gravity over the trench falls further below normal than anywhere else on Earth. The agency says this points to an active force pulling down on the area.

By the agency's reconstruction, a tilted layer of limestone starts more than four thousand feet above sea level. It ends about thirteen thousand feet below the surface. To the USGS, that tilt reflects big vertical shifts in this part of the trench and in Puerto Rico itself. Under the trench's deepest part, rotated blocks of rock indicate a sinking floor. That, the agency suggests, is why the trench is so deep. On the trench's walls, the agency's maps showed something else.

The USGS says those walls show many old underwater landslides, and that the risk of a tsunami set off by a landslide like those appears to be high. In October nineteen eighteen, an earthquake struck the Mona Passage, west of Puerto Rico. It wasn't in the trench. NOAA's tsunami database puts it at magnitude seven point one. Its tsunami ran as high as twenty feet up Puerto Rico's west coast. The quake and its tsunami killed more than one hundred people.

Farther east, an island holds a sign of what the trench itself can do. Anegada is a low island in the British Virgin Islands. Hundreds of coral boulders lie far inland there, along roughly six miles of its north shore, the side that faces the trench. By measuring the uranium in that coral, a twenty twenty-five study dated the tsunami that left them to sometime between thirteen eighty-one and thirteen ninety-one. That's about a century before Columbus reached the Caribbean.

The earthquake behind that wave struck the eastern part of this trench, far from its deepest point. Computer models put it at magnitude eight or more. The scientists who dated the coral call the wave the only known sign that this stretch of the trench has produced a quake that big. They think quakes like that come thousands of years apart.

In twenty fifteen, a NOAA robot filmed the trench's south wall, almost twenty thousand feet down. That's a long way east of its deepest point. The robot, Deep Discoverer, worked from the ship Okeanos Explorer, on one of a dozen dives it made on that voyage. Soon after, a problem with the robot cut this one short.

In December twenty eighteen, the Five Deeps Expedition came to map the trench with a modern multibeam sonar, on a ship called the Pressure Drop. The expedition's goal was to reach the deepest point of each of the five oceans. To get the sonar right, the team measured how fast sound travels at every depth, from the surface to the floor.

By the expedition's survey, the deepest point of the Atlantic is about twenty-seven thousand five hundred feet down. Give or take about sixteen feet. That point lies about eighty-three miles from the nearest coast of Puerto Rico, off Aguadilla, in the island's northwest. More than three million people live in Puerto Rico.

On Wednesday, December nineteenth, twenty eighteen, Victor Vescovo took a submersible called Limiting Factor down to the spot the sonar had just mapped. He made the trip alone, in his own sub, built to reach the bottom of any ocean. The trip down took about two and a half hours. He was the first person to reach the deepest point of the Atlantic. When he climbed out, a reporter on board heard him say: "One down!" The sub's own gauges confirmed the sonar's number, within about seven feet. That number was not the one in the official list.

In twenty nineteen, two scientists, Heather Stewart and Alan Jamieson, found that the official list of undersea features had the Milwaukee Deep at about twenty-eight thousand seven hundred feet. That's almost exactly what the newspapers reported in nineteen thirty-nine. The floor the expedition's sonar found is about one thousand two hundred feet shallower. And the USGS sonar had shown a shallower floor since two thousand three.

Stewart and Jamieson checked the published depths against sonar data that was already public. Off Puerto Rico, the real floor came out shallower every time. They wrote that numbers like these had spread, uncorrected, through online sources and the scientific literature. At the spot the old listing pointed to, their study found about twenty-four thousand four hundred feet, the top of a ridge.

Their study came out before the expedition's own results, and it put the deepest point somewhere else. Using public data from eight older surveys, it placed that point about thirty-six miles west of the sonar's spot, in the Dominican Republic's waters. The expedition's results, published in twenty twenty-one, placed it in U.S. waters off Puerto Rico, about one hundred miles from the Dominican Republic. Those U.S. waters are the exclusive economic zone, a band of sea where the U.S. controls the resources.

As of October twenty twenty-six, the official list of undersea features doesn't include the Milwaukee Deep. The expedition's scientists write that all of its sonar data went to Seabed twenty thirty, the project to map the whole ocean floor by twenty thirty. The expedition also took its sonar, and its sub, to the other end of the Atlantic.

The Atlantic has another contender for its deepest point: the South Sandwich Trench, far to the south, where one plate dives under another about three inches a year. That is three to four times the pace of the plates off Puerto Rico. The islands there are a chain of small volcanoes, with no permanent residents. In August twenty twenty-six, a Landsat satellite caught the heat of a lava lake in the crater of Mount Michael, one of those volcanoes.

The expedition mapped this trench with its sonar in twenty nineteen. Before that, about nine-tenths of it had never been mapped. Stewart and Jamieson's study noted the depth most often published for its deepest point. It was deeper than the sonar's number for Puerto Rico. The sonar settled that. The trench's deepest point, the Meteor Deep, is about three hundred seventy feet shallower than the one off Puerto Rico. The expedition mapped it but didn't dive there.

In twenty twenty-three, the International Hydrographic Organization recognized the Southern Ocean. It begins at sixty degrees south. The trench's southern tip crosses the line. By that line, the Meteor Deep, well to the north, is in the Atlantic. The organization says the line carries no political meaning, and not every country uses it. With the line or without it, the deepest point in the Atlantic lies north of the equator. Off Puerto Rico, the nineteen sixty-four crew's fish were waiting for a second look.

In twenty nineteen, the same sub went back to the spot where that crew had reported their fish. It was the craft that had carried Vescovo to the deepest point the year before. Where the nineteen sixty-four crew had counted about two hundred fish, it saw no snailfish. It found sea cucumbers instead, spread about as thickly as the fish the crew had reported. From the outside, the two look a lot alike in color, texture and shape.

In a twenty twenty paper on that return visit, five authors concluded that the "fish" of nineteen sixty-four were sea cucumbers. It's a conclusion drawn from the count and the look, and the animals the nineteen sixty-four crew saw that day can't be checked again. One of the five was Vescovo.

By NOAA's estimate, no fish lives much deeper than about twenty-seven thousand five hundred feet. The net that brought up the cusk-eel in nineteen seventy had gone down nearly that far. The deepest point in the Atlantic, about eighty-three miles off Puerto Rico, sits right at that edge.
